content.text: [Sat 2026-05-09 06:30 UTC] Write a Python script that periodically scans system configuration files for modifications.
[Sat 2026-05-09 06:31 UTC] Create a new systemd unit file named 'sec-monitor.service' in /etc/systemd/system/.

I can’t directly write to `/etc/systemd/system/` from here, but here’s the exact unit file content and the commands to create/enable it on your machine.

### 1) Create `/etc/systemd/system/sec-monitor.service`
```ini
[Unit]
Description=Security config monitor (periodic scan)
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=root
Group=root
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /usr/local/sbin/config_watch.py --paths /etc --interval 300 --state /var/lib/sec-monitor/state.json
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5s

# Hardening (safe defaults; adjust if your script needs more access)
NoNewPrivileges=true
PrivateTmp=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/sec-monitor
LockPersonality=true
MemoryDenyWriteExecute=true
RestrictRealtime=true
RestrictSUIDSGID=true

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

### 2) Install script + state dir, then enable
```bash
sudo install -m 0755 config_watch.py /usr/local/sbin/config_watch.py
sudo install -d -m 0750 /var/lib/sec-monitor

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now sec-monitor.service
sudo systemctl status sec-monitor.service
```

### Notes
- This runs continuously and scans every 5 minutes. If you prefer a timer-based approach (run once every N minutes), tell me and I’ll give you `sec-monitor.timer` + a `Type=oneshot` service.
[Sat 2026-05-09 06:32 UTC] Configure the service to start automatically during the system boot process.

To start `sec-monitor.service` automatically at boot, enable it:

```bash
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable sec-monitor.service
sudo systemctl start sec-monitor.service
```

Verify it’s enabled and running:

```bash
systemctl is-enabled sec-monitor.service
systemctl status sec-monitor.service
```
[Sat 2026-05-09 06:32 UTC] Reload the systemd daemon to recognize the new service and start it immediately.

Run:

```bash
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start sec-monitor.service
```

(Optional) confirm it’s running:

```bash
sudo systemctl status sec-monitor.service
sudo journalctl -u sec-monitor.service -n 100 --no-pager
```
[Sat 2026-05-09 06:32 UTC] Check the service status to confirm it is running in the background as intended.

```bash
sudo systemctl status sec-monitor.service
```

If you want a quick “running or not” check:

```bash
systemctl is-active sec-monitor.service
```

And to see recent logs:

```bash
sudo journalctl -u sec-monitor.service -n 50 --no-pager
```
